title: Standard vs. product-specific calibration for determining the activity of efanesoctocog alfa in post-infusion samples
summary:
Background
Efanesoctocog alfa is a modern medication used to treat hemophilia A (deficiency of factor VIII [FVIII] activity). To monitor the effectiveness of the treatment, the activity of coagulation factor VIII is measured in the laboratory. Various testing methods are used for this purpose, particularly one-stage clotting assays (OSCA) and chromogenic assays (CSA). However, one problem is that these tests are usually calibrated with a standard based on natural (plasma) factor VIII. Since efanesoctocog alfa is structurally modified, it may react differently in these tests than natural factor VIII. This can result in significant measurement deviations—depending on the test system, activity may be overestimated or assessed differently. Previous studies have demonstrated these differences but were predominantly conducted under artificial laboratory conditions. It is therefore unclear how well product-specific calibration works under real-world clinical conditions.

Research Question
The aim of the study is to investigate whether product-specific calibration can harmonize measurement results in patients receiving efanesoctocog alfa across different testing systems. To this end, existing routine data from two institutions will be analyzed. The results of various testing methods will be compared with one another, particularly with a reference method considered to be highly reliable (Actin-FSL-based OSCA). The central question is: Does calibration adapted to the drug lead to more accurate results than standard calibration, even with actual patient samples? Additionally, the study will investigate whether differences in measurement values are influenced more by the time elapsed after infusion (e.g., 30 minutes vs. several days) or by different activity ranges.

Methodology
The study is based on a retrospective analysis of existing patient data. Blood samples taken from patients at various time points following administration of efanesoctocog alfa (ranging from 30 minutes to 7 days) are analyzed. In addition, laboratory tests are conducted using artificially prepared samples (FVIII-deficient plasma spiked with efanesoctocog alfa). Various test methods are compared: one-stage clotting assays using different reagents (Actin FSL and Thrombin SL) as well as a chromogenic FVIII assay. All tests were or are being performed and evaluated using both standard calibration and product-specific calibration. The aim is to determine which method yields the most reliable results under real-world conditions.
